newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil Febec coffee body to discuss re-structuring.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Febec coffee body to discuss re-structuring.

text.p: Officials from Brazil's Coffee Exporters' Federation (Febec) are to meet July 14 in Vitoria, Espirito Santo state, to discuss a re-structuring of the entity, said Febec president Oswaldo Aranha.
Febec is Brazil's traditional exporting body but in November 1995 a group of exporters formed Abecafe, principally because they opposed a plan dividing out exports internally.
The association has grown in size and now has 45 members, accounting for around 47 percent of Brazilian coffee exports in 1996, according to Abecafe statistics.
Aranha however, as president of Febec, holds the one place for exporters on Brazil's coffee council, which unites the public and private sectors and this has been a point of contention for Abecafe.
At the beginning of May a six-member Febec/Abecafe committee began talks to see if it were possible to create a new entity which would unite the two groups.

However talks have advanced little, with one of the key points of divergence whether any new entity should be a federation of existing coffee associations (as sought by Febec) or a body made up of export companies (as prefered by Abecafe).
Febec elections, due to have been held at the end of April, were postponed to allow for a possible outcome from the talks.
But now Febec should go ahead and look at changing its own statutes before holding elections by the end of this month, Aranha said.
At the meeting next week, officials will discuss suggestions made by Aranha which would make Febec more of a federation which deals with associations and without direct links with companies.
One proposed change is a system in which council seats would be decided according to the number of bags shipped by each regional center, with associations then nominating their own representatives.
Each association's exports would not be determined by the amount shipped from ports in the region but by total shipments by its members.
Therefore exports by the Vitoria association for example would include all coffee shipped by members out of any port in Brazil and not just Vitoria.
Likewise coffee shipped out of Vitoria by a company which belonged to the Rio de Janeiro association would not be counted in Vitoria's exports.
"This is even more democratic than before," Aranha said.
Currently the council is comprised of 35 companies which are agreed by consensus. The companies then nominate their representatives to sit on the council, a Febec official said.
Aranha hopes that, if approved, the changes in the statutes will be regarded favorably by Abecafe.

But given Abecafe wants an organisation made up of individual companies and not associations, the proposed changes would not appear to bring the two groups nearer together, said Jorge Esteve, Abecafe president.

Elsewhere this week, traders were still monitoring the quality of new crop coffees which are showing the effects of last month's rains. The recent dry spell however has done much to help the drying process and traders are more optimistic.
The delays in the harvesting and the impact on quality has not led to any defaults on deliveries of coffee against the rural product bonds (CPRs), a Banco do Brasil official said.
The CPRs involve bank backing for advance sales of coffee to domestic or export customers at pre-established prices.
In total some 180,000 bags have been sold through CPRs for delivery from July to October, 20,000 bags of which are for July, the official said.
The quality of coffee is certified by the BM&F exchange in Sao Paulo and so far Parana coffees have if anything been above the required qualities, he added.

Coffees from Patrocinio in the Cerrado region of Minas Gerais have reached the required standard after some mixing while in the south of Minas, there have been some problems but these contracts have been liquidated by mutual agreement.
((-- Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151))
